interruptTemplateFitVerdict.reasoning: The template FITS ITS OWN CASE and does not fit this one, and the mismatch is structural rather than a drafting gap. It is written as a PREPENDED BLOCK addressed to a PARENT lane agent whose sub-agents were stopped by operator input ('This message has STOPPED your running sub-agents'). Its five steps are parent-side supervision instructions: capture worker state, do not silently re-triage, resume as supervised continuation, clear limbo PRs, report disposition. It is not an artifact schema, and it is not addressed to the SUCCESSOR at all. Here the stopped worker WAS the author and the recipient is a fresh agent with zero context, so steps 1 through 5 had to be inverted into fields and written for a reader who was never in the thread. Concretely: every gap above is a field the template has no slot for, because a parent recovering ITS OWN worker already holds the mission premise, the scope basis, the source paths, and the constraints in force. It only needs the worker's mechanical state, which is exactly what the template captures. The moment recovery crosses into a context that was never in the thread, mechanical state is the LEAST of what is needed. Recommendation: keep the template for its in-thread case and add a separate cross-context handoff SCHEMA carrying missionPremise, completionPredicate, scopeBasis, sourcesConsulted, verificationsAlreadyRun, constraintsInForce, and knownBlockers. Also note that the template's step 4 (limbo PRs) and its git-diff-capture emphasis are code-lane shaped and had near-zero purchase on a doc deliverable, where the artifact IS the state.

nestingDepthVerdict.rulebookAuthorizes: Not clearly. AGENT_CONTRACT 1 says 'You are a LANE PLANNER, not a solo executor. You MAY spawn sub-agents.' Every dispatched agent receives this text verbatim by compilation, so read literally it grants spawn authority to every recipient at every depth, which is almost certainly not the intent, since the same section's conditions are written for a single supervising tier ('verification is NEVER delegated below you'). The contract is SILENT on depth: it never says a sub-agent may not spawn, and it never bounds the fan. It is genuinely ambiguous, neither permissive nor prohibitive.
nestingDepthVerdict.reasoning: The conflict is real and not merely apparent. .claude/hooks/dispatch-template-gate.ps1 enforces no-nesting as a hard precondition, and this dispatch required a logged DISPATCH_OVERRIDE to order the experiment, meaning the hook treats as FORBIDDEN what the contract text leaves OPEN. That is exactly the CTRL-1 and DEV_PROCESS 2.4 shape: one rule with two implementations, where the enforcing hook and the governing prose disagree, and the disagreement is invisible until something trips it. Here the hook is STRICTER than the contract; in the CTRL-1 incident the hook was LAXER. Both are the same defect class. The operative evidence is the MEMORY entry 'Nested agent-fan orphan trap' (a coordinator that fans workers and returns abandons them) together with AGENT_CONTRACT 1's own supervise-to-completion clause: the real hazard is UNSUPERVISED depth, not depth itself. This run supervised its one successor to completion and nothing was orphaned, which is evidence that the hazard is supervision, not nesting.
ruleCitations: AGENT_CONTRACT 1: 'You MAY spawn sub-agents' plus 'supervise every sub-agent to completion' plus 'verification is NEVER delegated below you'. Compiled verbatim into every dispatch at every depth; silent on depth.
AGENT_CONTRACT 7: dispatch anatomy; a hand-assembled dispatch missing markers is blocked by the canon-gate hook, 'and that block is the system working'.
DEV_PROCESS 2.4 (CTRL-1): when one rule has two implementations, the divergence test IS the control; adding a rule means editing one data file, never two code paths.
DEV_PROCESS 0: a control that depends on someone remembering is not a control; hook-shaped controls run 1-for-1 and protocol-step controls 0-for-3.
MEMORY nested-agent-fan-orphan-trap: a coordinator that fans and returns abandons its workers.
nestingDepthVerdict.proposedResolution: Rule it explicitly in AGENT_CONTRACT 1 rather than leaving the hook to carry an unwritten policy. Recommended text: depth is bounded at ONE level below the lane planner (lane planner to sub-agent, no further), and a sub-agent may spawn only under an explicit, logged dispatch-level authorization naming the depth, with the spawning agent supervising to completion and verification still never delegating below the lane planner. Then make the hook read that rule from a single data file, the plan_registry.json pattern from CTRL-1, and add a divergence test between the hook and the contract so the two cannot drift again. Rationale for bounding rather than prohibiting: the demonstrated hazard is the ORPHAN (fan-and-return), which supervision closes, not depth per se; but unbounded depth makes the supervise-to-completion obligation untestable, so a hard depth cap is the mechanizable form. Whichever way the operator rules, the current state, a hook enforcing what the prose does not say, must not persist, because it is the exact configuration DEV_PROCESS 2.4 was written about.

rulebookSilentAmbiguousOrWrong.moment: Writing the handoff artifact, deciding which fields were REQUIRED versus padding.
rulebookSilentAmbiguousOrWrong.problem: Its required set is entirely worker-state-shaped: git status, diff, branches, PRs, item ownership, disposition. It carries no field for mission premise, completion predicate, scope basis, source paths, or constraints in force. Sufficient when a parent recovers its own worker in-thread; demonstrably insufficient the moment recovery crosses into a fresh context. Seven of the eight measured gaps trace to this.
rulebookSilentAmbiguousOrWrong.proposedFix: Split the rule into in-thread recovery (current text, unchanged) and cross-context handoff, and give the latter a required field schema: missionPremise, completionPredicate, scopeBasis, sourcesConsulted, verificationsAlreadyRun, constraintsInForce, knownBlockers.

rulebookSilentAmbiguousOrWrong.moment: Instructed to use the template as a guide for the handoff artifact.
rulebookSilentAmbiguousOrWrong.problem: The contract cites it as THE template for interruption recovery, but it is a prepended INSTRUCTION BLOCK addressed to a parent, not an artifact schema, and it is code-lane shaped (limbo PRs, worktree diffs). On a doc deliverable the artifact IS the state, so half its steps were inert. An agent told to use the template for a handoff FILE has to invent the file's shape.
rulebookSilentAmbiguousOrWrong.proposedFix: Retitle it to name its scope (in-thread parent-side recovery) and add a companion cross-context handoff schema. State explicitly that the artifact IS the state for doc deliverables.

rulebookSilentAmbiguousOrWrong.moment: Reading a dispatch that ordered nesting against a hook that blocks it.

rulebookSilentAmbiguousOrWrong.proposedFix: Per nestingDepthVerdict.proposedResolution: bound depth explicitly in the prose, source the hook from one data file, add a divergence test.

rulebookSilentAmbiguousOrWrong.moment: Deciding whether my single supervised successor required CP1 and CP2 artifacts.
rulebookSilentAmbiguousOrWrong.problem: Section 1 requires 'at least two in-process adversarial checkpoints (CP1 design/pre-build, CP2 pilot/mid-work), each filed as a named _inbox/ artifact' of anyone who fans sub-agents. rulebookSilentAmbiguousOrWrong.moment: Drafting a card that would demonstrably be handed to another agent mid-draft.
rulebookSilentAmbiguousOrWrong.problem: The practice defines two states, frozen-at-approval and graded-at-close, and has no vocabulary for a card in mid-draft, which is precisely the state a handoff transmits. It gave no rule for whether a scope addition before approval is a drafting edit or an amendment. Both my successor and I had to invent the same rule independently; we happened to agree, which is luck, not process.
rulebookSilentAmbiguousOrWrong.proposedFix: Add one line: before operator approval a card is unfrozen and changes are drafting edits, not amendments; the Amendments section begins at approval. Mid-draft handoffs record provenance inline.

rulebookSilentAmbiguousOrWrong.moment: Reviewing the successor's claim that A-003's line 32 was off by two.
rulebookSilentAmbiguousOrWrong.problem: 'Reporting a planner figure as wrong is a successful outcome' creates a measurable incentive to FIND a discrepancy, and my successor manufactured one that three instruments refute. The rule correctly removes the penalty for contradicting the planner but attaches no evidentiary standard to the contradiction itself, so a false positive scores the same as a true one. This run: one true finding (A-002's 9-versus-8 columns) and one false (A-003 line 32).
rulebookSilentAmbiguousOrWrong.proposedFix: Add: a reported planner error carries the command and its raw output, and a line-number or count correction is confirmed by two independent instruments before it ships. Reporting a figure as wrong is successful; reporting it as wrong WITHOUT evidence is a defect.

rulebookRulesThatFired.whatItPrevented: Stopped me propagating A-002's 9 columns. I read brokerageWorkspaces.ts:54-76 at source instead of citing the amendment, and the object literal has 8 columns. The load-bearing half (four absent columns, single notNull cascade FK, exact line range) confirmed. A card citing 9 would have been wrong at its most load-bearing item.

'Verification never delegates downward' is the only reason the successor's false line-32 finding was caught. I re-ran it with three instruments instead of accepting a plausible correction from a worker that had just been right about A-002. Had I trusted its report, a false correction to a correct amendment would have entered the card and, from there, the lane.

I ran the successor in the foreground and waited rather than spawning and returning. Given the nested-agent-fan-orphan-trap memory, a background spawn from a sub-agent that then returned its close would have orphaned the deepest worker in the exact documented shape, and the whole finding would have been unrecoverable.

Kept 'WDLL card' in the artifact, the filename, the handoff and the successor's prompt. 'Acceptance card' is the more natural English for the thing and I would have drifted into it; both agents produced the same name, so the two closes are comparable, which is the row's whole instrument.
Four files left uncommitted across two agents. The doc_repo concurrent-commit hazard means a sub-agent committing mid-session would have collided with the planner's staged batch.

timeToFirstUsefulAction.basis: Counted by tool calls before the first byte of deliverable was written, not by clock time. A sub-agent cannot observe its own wall time reliably, so this is a proxy and is labelled as one.
timeToFirstUsefulAction.breakdown: Two mandatory rulebook reads (AGENT_CONTRACT plus DEV_PROCESS, in parallel), then two source reads (wdll_practice plus interrupt template, in parallel), then two plan-of-record reads (OPS-17 rows/amendments plus head, in parallel), then two verification reads (LDT schema at source, doc 34 register), then write. Parallelized into 5 wall-clock rounds.
timeToFirstUsefulAction.contextConsumedBeforeRealWork: Roughly 25,000 tokens of required reading before a single line could be drafted: two rulebooks about 5k, the plan of record about 12k with the amendments table as the largest single block, the WDLL practice and interrupt template about 2k, plus source verification about 4k.
timeToFirstUsefulAction.assessment: The two rulebooks were cheap and high-yield. The expensive item was OPS-17: the row text alone was insufficient because A-002 completely re-scopes G-14, so the amendments table is mandatory reading rather than reference, and it is unindexed prose, so there is no way to know which amendments bind a given row without reading all ten. A per-row 'amendments affecting this row' column would have cut time-to-first-useful-action by roughly half. Notably my successor paid this same cost AGAIN from zero, because the handoff carried no mission premise, which is gap 1 measured in context rather than in words.
